summary: Specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Dense Mode (PIM-DM), a multicast routing protocol that uses unicast routing information and floods multicast datagrams to all multicast routers. Prune messages stop later packets from reaching routers with no group members. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Send a message to every street first, then streets with nobody interested say stop sending it here.

questions: how does pim-dm flood and prune work
what is a graft message in pim-dm
subtitle: Flood multicast traffic everywhere first, then let routers with no interested members prune their branches off.

tldr.problem: Multicast groups that are densely spread across a network need a routing method that does not depend on a particular topology discovery protocol or on a central rendezvous point.
tldr.mechanism: PIM-DM assumes every downstream router wants the traffic, floods it using reverse path forwarding (RPF) checks, and lets routers send Prune messages for branches with no group members. Graft messages restore a pruned branch, and State Refresh messages keep prune state alive.
tldr.outcome: The design is simple but causes flooding and pruning on some links that better topology information could avoid. It is an Experimental RFC, and later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 3973 is an Experimental RFC, not an Internet Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

sections.title: Flood and Prune
sections.content:
RFC 3973 specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Dense Mode (PIM-DM), a multicast routing protocol for groups that are densely distributed across a network. It uses the unicast routing information that already exists, in a table the RFC calls the Multicast Routing Information Base (MRIB), and has no topology discovery mechanism of its own. It reuses the packet formats of sparse mode PIM (PIM-SM).

PIM-DM assumes that when a source starts sending, all downstream systems want the datagrams. Traffic is first flooded to all areas of the network, and reverse path forwarding (RPF) prevents loops. Where an area has no group members, a router creates prune state to cut off that branch. Prune state has a finite lifetime, so data flows again when it expires. This cycle is the flood and prune cycle typical of dense mode protocols.

Compared with protocols that include topology discovery, such as DVMRP, the design is simpler and more flexible, but it floods and prunes some links that could be avoided. The RFC accepts that extra overhead on purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: First the message goes everywhere. Then places that do not want it say no thanks, and after a while it is tried again in case they changed their minds.

sections.title: State and Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
Traffic is identified by an (S,G) pair: source S and destination group G. The upstream interface is the one toward the source (the RPF interface), and the downstream interfaces are all the others. A router keeps a Tree Information Base (TIB) with per-interface neighbor state and per-(S,G) prune, assert and graft state. The RFC says this is abstract state, and an implementation only has to behave the same way externally.

When a data packet arrives, the router first performs an RPF check. A packet that fails the check MUST NOT be forwarded, and the router runs the assert process. If a route to the source cannot be found, the packet MUST be discarded. If the check passes, the router builds an outgoing interface list from neighbors, local group members learned through IGMP and other membership mechanisms, minus pruned interfaces, lost asserts and scope boundaries. If the list is empty, the router starts a prune process for that (S,G).
sections.plainLanguage: A router only accepts a copy from the direction it would use to reach the sender, which stops copies from circling forever. Then it passes the copy on to every neighbor who has not said no.

sections.title: Prune, Join, Graft and State Refresh
sections.content:
When a router has nothing to forward for an (S,G), it sends a Prune upstream. The upstream router does not cut off the branch at once if it has more than one neighbor on that interface. It enters a PrunePending state for a short time, the J/P_Override_Interval, so another router on the same LAN can send a Join to override the Prune. With only one neighbor on the interface, it SHOULD set the timer to zero and prune immediately.

When a new member appears in a pruned area, the router sends a Graft toward the source and keeps retrying until it receives a Graft Ack, which is unicast to the Graft's originator. This turns the pruned branch back into a forwarding branch.

To avoid repeated flooding, routers directly connected to the source periodically send State Refresh messages, which are propagated through the network and refresh existing prune state. Forwarding of these messages is rate limited.
sections.plainLanguage: If a street says no thanks, the mail carrier waits a moment in case a neighbor shouts wait, we want it. If someone moves in later, they can ask for the mail again with a Graft, and State Refresh is a reminder that the street still says no.

sections.title: Hellos, Asserts and Timers
sections.content:
Routers find each other with Hello messages, multicast to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group on each PIM-enabled interface every Hello_Period, 30 sec by default. The first Hello is delayed by a random time up to Triggered_Hello_Delay (5 sec) so routers powered on together do not synchronize. The Hold Time in a Hello is normally 3.5 times Hello_Period. A Hold Time of 0xffff means never time out, and 0 means expire at once. A changed Generation ID means the neighbor has restarted.

If two routers on a LAN both forward the same (S,G) traffic, they run an Assert election. Compared are the metric preference and route metric, where the lower value wins, and the highest IP address breaks ties. When all routers on a LAN use the LAN Prune Delay option they use the largest values on the LAN. Otherwise the Override Interval MUST be 2.5 seconds and the Propagation Delay 0.5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers say hello to each other every so often to show they are still there. If two of them both try to deliver the same thing to a street, they compare notes and the better one keeps the job.

sections.title: Differences from PIM-SM and Interactions
sections.content:
PIM-DM differs from sparse mode in two essential ways. There are no periodic joins, only explicitly triggered prunes and grafts, and there is no Rendezvous Point (RP). That matters in networks that cannot tolerate a single point of failure.

PIM-DM is not intended to interact directly with PIM-SM, even though the packet format is shared, and a router cannot tell a PIM-DM neighbor from a PIM-SM one by Hello messages. If they become neighbors, they effectively form a simplex link, with the PIM-DM router sending all multicast to the PIM-SM router and getting none back. A Prune is not permitted to stop delivery to a network that has group members. PIM-DM routers MUST NOT send any messages about a group across that group's scope boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Dense mode and sparse mode speak similar languages but have different ideas, so they should not be mixed on the same neighbor links.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IPsec Authentication Header MAY be used to protect PIM messages. A router SHOULD NOT process PIM messages from a neighbor until it has received a valid Hello from it. PIM-DM has no rendezvous point and therefore no single point of failure, but it relies on unicast routes from some other routing protocol and can suffer if that protocol is attacked.

The RFC walks through forged messages. Forged Hello, Join, Prune or Graft messages can waste bandwidth by drawing traffic to links with no real receivers. A forged Assert on a multi-access LAN can make the legitimate forwarder stop forwarding, and forged State Refresh messages can be propagated downstream in a denial of service attack, so a PIM-DM router SHOULD rate limit the State Refresh messages it propagates.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pretend to be a neighbor and send fake messages, wasting bandwidth or cutting off a street. So routers should check who they are talking to and not repeat suspicious reminders too fast.
